rv.q: This new play by Jessica Dickey, directed with grace and dignity by Marti Lyons, is bewitching and enthralling.
Ultimately, this lovely and deeply philosophical (not to mention educational) play, at its core, is a reflection of Galileo's most famous invention, the telescope.
Lyons skillfully squeezes her small cast into its many characters and gives a premiere to an intriguing play that may still face revisions, but is very much worth seeing today.
Johnson fills the play with a village of distinct and memorable personalities and he is a joy to watch, as he supports the two female leads.
Still, the show is an enjoyable intro into Galileo and his family.
This is a highly romantic story with, as I said, an ending that will be pleasing to the audience members.

cn.t: Critics praise this smart, complex world premiere for its inventive structure interweaving past and present, as a playwright researching Galileo's daughter in Florence finds parallels to her own life in under 85 minutes.
